questions.question: A capability is adopted heavily by the customers who requested it, and those accounts cost more to serve than they return. Which hypothesis failed?
options: Problem — the requested need was not real
Value — the capability does not work well enough
Economics — value captured does not exceed cost to serve at this unit
Retention — usage will decay once novelty fades
questions.explanation: Adoption supports problem and value; the failure is below them in the chain. B is the tempting answer because teams reach for a product-quality explanation first, but a capability can work exactly as intended and still be unaffordable to deliver.

questions.question: Noted's PM writes the audience hypothesis as "enterprise team leads who run recurring meetings." Why is this not yet usable?
options: It is a label, and the product does not capture meeting type, so no one in the product can be identified as a member
Enterprise is too small a population to build a strategy on
It names a role rather than a company size band
Recurring meetings are a behaviour of the team, not of the lead
questions.explanation: An audience hypothesis has to be stated by observable behaviour, and the case says meeting type is not captured at all. D is tempting and half-true, but the fatal problem is not whose behaviour it is — it is that no available data can sort anyone into or out of the group.

questions.question: Which pairing of hypothesis and evidence type is correct?
options: Value — satisfaction scores from users of the capability
Retention — a claim about how often the underlying job recurs
Problem — the number of inbound requests received this quarter
Acquisition — interview quotes about why customers like the product
questions.explanation: Retention rests on recurrence: if the job does not come back, no amount of product quality produces return usage. A is the tempting distractor, because satisfaction is easy to collect and feels like value evidence, but value is a comparison against the alternative the person uses now, not a rating of your product.

questions.question: A team must choose what to test next. Which hypothesis should decide that choice?
options: The one with the most existing data, so the test can run quickly
The one the executive team asks about most often
The one where confidence is high and consequence-if-false is high
The one where confidence is low and consequence-if-false is high
questions.explanation: Low confidence plus high consequence is where the strategy is actually exposed. A is what most teams do, because progress is fastest where instrumentation already exists — but testing a well-evidenced link mostly reconfirms what you already believe.

questions.question: A collaboration product tests retention on single-user accounts and finds it weak. What does the boundary of this model say?
options: The retention hypothesis is disproved and the position should be abandoned
Value and retention are coupled here, so the test unit should be a team rather than a user
The result is valid but should be weighted less because the sample is small
Retention should be re-tested after acquisition improves
questions.explanation: When value depends on other participants, a single-user test measures a condition the strategy never claimed would work. A is the tempting reading — it treats a precise number as a decisive one, which is exactly the error the coupling boundary warns about.
